title: Garry Tan, 'Own Your Intelligence' — Y Combinator Startup School 2026 keynote on Personal AGI and skill-file ownership
author: Garry Tan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Tan accepts the cluster’s core view that model capability alone does not create value and materially extends its operating-model argument by identifying owned, well-governed context repositories as a source of differentiation. His account of capturing, linking, prioritising and reconciling knowledge adds concrete detail to the cluster’s emphasis on authoritative knowledge and workflow design, though it is a general and largely predictive argument rather than legal-specific evidence.
qs: The better the models get, the more the differentiator moves to context.
What gets written down in the first place, how it gets enriched and linked, what gets promoted to hot memory versus filed as cold cold reference, who arbitrates when two facts disagree.

mo.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks

kp.k: Personal AGI combines owned context with rented models
kp.d: Tan defines personal AGI as an agent operating on an individual's infrastructure, memory and procedures, rather than a universally achieved intelligence threshold or subscription chatbot. His cross-domain argument is that accumulated personal context makes this an appreciating asset rather than merely a consumed product; the keynote does not discuss legal services directly.
qs: AGI isn't arriving as an event, it's arriving diffused as your agent running on your context, doing your work.
An agent that runs on your infrastructure, reads from a memory you own, executes procedures you wrote, and compounds.
One of these is a product you consume. The other is an asset you build.

kp.k: Productivity multipliers rest on personal estimates and portfolio observations
kp.d: Tan reports approximately 14 useful lines of code daily while building Bookface in 2013 and estimates his current output at about 400x, with an asserted 8x floor after allowances for verbosity and scaffolding. He extends the productivity argument to all knowledge work. As portfolio evidence, he says a quarter of winter 25 companies had 95% AI-generated codebases and that the batch is on track for exceptional growth and profitability, explicitly declining to claim causation.
qs: I shipped maybe 14 useful lines of code a day
I'm at about 400x what I did in 2013.
It's still 8x at the absolute floor, and 10 times that in the middle of the range.
a quarter of the companies had codebases that were 95% AI generated.
I cannot prove that the AI generated code and everything else caused the growth
It's for every piece of knowledge work.

kp.k: Context selection differentiates users of identical models
kp.d: Tan argues that differences between modest and very large productivity gains arise from relevant context delivered at the right workflow step, not just model weights. He contrasts human working memory, described as seven plus or minus two items, with a million-token agent context window, while emphasizing that even roughly 1,000 pages cannot contain an entire life. His proposed solution is a library plus a librarian that selects the relevant material.
qs: There are 2X people and there are 100X people who are using the same cloud, same weights, same context window size, same API
It's in what context you give it, how relevant it is, and does it happen at the right step.
An AI agent, though, holds a million tokens.
Who decides or what decides which three books are open on the desk?
The library plus the librarian.

kp.k: Persistent memory supports proactive, contextual administrative work
kp.d: Tan describes his own G brain as approximately 220,000 markdown pages covering 25 years of personal and professional history, largely compiled and curated by agents. His reported uses include overnight inbox processing, contextual briefings, meeting preparation, research and monitoring relevant developments. These are accounts of his operating practices, not independently evaluated outcomes.
qs: My personal open claw has a Karpathy-style knowledge wiki with about 220,000 markdown pages. 25 years of my life diarized.
Compiled mostly by agents, curated by agents, searched for by agents.
I wake up to a briefing, not a pile of emails.
Before every meeting, a prep doc, who I'm meeting, what we said last time, what changed since and what I should ask.

kp.k: Skill files turn written procedures into executable workflows
kp.d: Tan presents markdown skill files as plain-English procedures that agents can execute using tools. His example processes meeting recordings, extracts commitments and deadlines, links people to existing records and flags contradictions without overwriting them. He reports that YC media, events and finance staff are building such workflows, including a finance worker combining about a hundred Excel workbooks into an app, and predicts a general shift toward managing agents.
qs: If anything contradicts something we already believe, flag it. Don't overwrite it.
If a smart intern could follow it, an agent can run it.
If you can write clear instructions in English, you're a programmer. The compiler is a language model.
One of our finance folks compiled um about a hundred Excel workbooks into a single app she built with an internal agent.
She is a manager of agents now. Everyone is about to be.

kp.k: Reliable workflows combine model judgment with deterministic computation
kp.d: Tan distinguishes tasks he assigns to model inference, such as taste, judgment and interpreting vague requests, from arithmetic, SQL queries and other operations requiring deterministic execution. He uses the conference's custom schedules for 6,000 people as an example of markdown instructions calling databases and scripts rather than relying on model reasoning alone.
qs: Some computation belongs in latent space. Taste, judgment, reading what a human actually wants from a vague request.
And then some computation belongs in deterministic space. The arithmetic, the SQL query.
Ask it to make custom schedules for 6,000 people in an arena, like we just did for you, and your latent space agent needs to write some code to keep track of it.
The latent and the deterministic markdown files calling databases and scripts.

kp.k: Research agents produce contextual synthesis for human editing
kp.d: Tan reports using an overnight compendium workflow to process three Spinoza biographies by Nadler, Goldstein and Stewart, about 1,500 pages, five days before the talk. He says it produced a chronology, disagreements among biographers, quotations with chapter citations and ten ranked storytelling moments with delivery notes. He describes the result as material he could edit, rather than reporting a formal accuracy assessment.
qs: books by Nadler, Goldstein, and Stewart, about 1,500 pages.
It built me a synthesis, a dated chronology of his life, every place the three biographers disagree with each other, and the best verbatim quotes with chapter citations.
1,500 pages became a stage-ready story that I could edit.

kp.k: Agent workforces enable smaller organizations and personalized software
kp.d: Tan analogizes skill files to employees and routing mechanisms to organizational charts, arguing that one founder can manage an organization of agents before incorporation. He cites Emergent from summer 24 reaching nine figures of revenue within eight months of public launch and having 15 people at $15 million annualized revenue; he also cites “Retail winter 24” reaching 60 million annualized with about 40 people. These examples support his claim of changed company economics and cheaper tools for an audience of one, some of which may become businesses.
qs: A skill file is an employee.
A resolver is an org chart.
Emergent out of our summer 24 batch went from public launch to nine figures of revenue in eight months.
When they crossed $15 million in annualized revenue, they were 15 people. Retail winter 24 hit 60 million annualized with about 40.
You can build exactly the tool you need for the audience of one in a weekend.

kp.k: Memory quality requires provenance, contradiction checks and pruning
kp.d: Tan qualifies his enthusiasm by warning that uncurated memory can confidently surface stale facts and that poor skill files preserve defective processes. He recommends provenance for every fact, contradiction handling and active pruning. He also argues that retrieval alone is not the product: selecting, enriching, linking and prioritizing knowledge, and resolving disagreement, determine whether memory is useful.
qs: a brain nobody curates is a garbage dump with great search.
Retrieval will surface a stale fact with total confidence. A bad skill file encodes a bad process forever.
the primitive is memory plus hygiene, provenance on every fact, contradiction contradiction checks when new information collides with old, and a librarian whose actual job is pruning.
Retrieval is easy. Being worth retrieving from is the product.

kp.k: Reusable workflows accumulate through correction and recurring execution
kp.d: Tan recommends running an agent, starting a small contextual library, writing and correcting one skill, scheduling it and converting completed tasks into reusable procedures. He predicts a 90-day progression from a clumsy first-week toy to useful contextual outputs by week four and approximately a dozen workflows by week 12. This is an adoption prescription and forecast, not a reported longitudinal study.
qs: Every rule, every exception, every oh and also, put it in there and it'll fix it.
At the end of every task, ask the agent to skillify what it did.
Week one, honestly, it's a toy. The library is thin. The skills are clumsy. You're fixing more than you're saving.
Week four, the flywheel catches.
A dozen skill files running the parts of your week you used to dread, and one or two tools that other people keep asking to borrow.

kp.k: Skill ownership determines worker accumulation versus employer extraction
kp.d: Tan argues that executable procedures externalize workers' judgment, making control of those files central to career autonomy. In his explicitly fictional example, support engineer Maya develops 40 skills over two years: personal control permits accumulated expertise to travel between jobs, whereas company control allows continued execution after she leaves with nothing. His statement that skills belong to workers is a normative doctrine, not a legal finding about ownership.
qs: Take a fictional example of a support engineer.
Over two years, Maya teaches her agents 40 skills.
Version one, those files live in Maya's repo. She changes jobs, they go with her.
Version two, those files live in the company's repo under the company's IT policy. Maya leaves with nothing.
The company keeps running her judgment without her.
I believe skill files are yours. Own your skills because if you don't, your job becomes a skill file.

kp.k: Model improvements increase the value of proprietary context
kp.d: Responding to the objection that improving models will make harnesses obsolete, Tan argues that increasingly capable, widely available models shift differentiation toward owned context. He portrays each model release as an upgrade to an existing agent workforce and an increase in the value of its accumulated library.
qs: The better the models get, the more the differentiator moves to context.
A better model makes your library worth more because a smarter reader extracts more from the same books.
every release they ship is a free upgrade to a workforce I already own

kp.k: Personal custody is Tan's answer to concentrated privacy risk
kp.d: Tan acknowledges the objection that consolidating email, meetings and family schedules creates a potential leak exposure. He answers by advocating personally controlled infrastructure, repositories and keys, contrasting this with information scattered across corporate clouds. This is his security argument; the transcript supplies no comparative security assessment.
qs: You put your entire life in one system, your email, your meetings, your kids schedules. What happens when it leaks?
My brain runs on my own infra, in my own repo, under my own keys.
I didn't create the risk by consolidating my context. I took custody of it.
Custody is the security model

kp.k: Open infrastructure is proposed to democratize agent capabilities
kp.d: Tan justifies releasing his harness, memory architecture and skills openly as distributing tools otherwise available to powerful actors. He asserts that the capability gap between those with agent infrastructure and those without it is widening monthly, and frames open distribution as a means of avoiding concentrated control.
qs: I believe tools of the powerful should be given away.
The people who have it are quietly operating at at different scale than the people who don't.
And the gap is widening every month.
When something like that, that powerful stays private, you get a priesthood. When it gets given away, you get a renaissance.

kp.k: Personal research libraries can support specialized family care
kp.d: Tan recounts a friend building an 80,000-file repository concerning his son's rare epilepsy, linking specialist visits, papers, seizure logs and drug interactions. He presents rapid identification of previously tried ideas as an example of personally directed research without a lab or grant; he does not report a clinical outcome.
qs: I have a friend whose son has a rare form of epilepsy.
He built a repo of 80,000 markdown files.
Every specialist visit, every paper, every seizure log, every drug interaction, indexed and cross-linked and ready.
So that when a new doctor has an idea, he knows in minutes whether it's already been tried.

kp.k: Spinoza frames agent ownership as increased power to act
kp.d: Tan uses Spinoza's striving and definitions of joy and sadness as a theoretical frame for increased or diminished agency. He draws a historical analogy between craftsmen owning tools, factory owners controlling looms and employers potentially owning externalized cognition. His conclusion is that personal AGI should preserve self-direction, with entrepreneurship offered as a way to make owned skills work for their creator.
qs: Conatus. It means your striving, the drive in every living thing to keep going and to increase its power to act.
In Ethics, he defines joy as the feeling of your power of acting increasing
Craftsmen own their tools. That's what made them free. The factory broke that. The loom belonged to the mill.
Personal AGI is how you stay under your own power in the age of agents.
keep your brain and your skills in a repo you control from day one before any platform or any acquirer has an opinion about it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Garry Tan claims that personally controlled, context-rich agents already multiply knowledge-work output, enable very small businesses, and make executable expertise an asset whose ownership determines whether workers benefit or are displaced.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain keynote about startups, software, knowledge work and personal information management; Tan makes no specific claims about legal services. He defines 'personal AGI' as an agent operating on user-controlled infrastructure, memory and procedures, rather than as a universal intelligence threshold. He claims that persistent context and reusable skills make these systems compound with use, while model capabilities are rented commodities. Tan reports roughly 400-fold growth in his own coding output relative to 2013, proposing an eightfold floor after hypothetical discounts, and extends the productivity-multiplier claim to design, product management, growth and all knowledge work. He argues that the best-performing founders use agents as a workforce rather than autocomplete, allowing one person to operate an organization and small teams to achieve exceptional revenues. Clear English instructions become executable 'skill files', so nonprogrammers can build software and manage agents. Cheap custom software can be built for an audience of one, with some tools subsequently becoming startups. He further claims that ownership of accumulated context and skills becomes a central source of competitive differentiation: better models increase the value of a proprietary library. Conversely, employer-controlled skill files can preserve and execute a worker's judgment after that worker leaves. His assertion that skill files should belong to individuals is a normative ownership doctrine, not an account of existing legal ownership rights. He also presents personal research libraries as enabling individuals to navigate specialized information, illustrated by a father researching his son's epilepsy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Tan supports his claims with personal experience, YC portfolio observations, named company examples, internal workflow anecdotes and a fictional ownership scenario, rather than a presented controlled study or benchmark.
pts.d: For productivity, Tan compares his reported output of about 14 useful lines of code per day while building Bookface in 2013 with his present output while running YC. His adjustments for verbosity, scaffolding and self-flattery are hypothetical sensitivity discounts, not independently measured productivity estimates. At portfolio level, he reports that a quarter of the winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated and says that batch is on track to be among YC's fastest-growing and most profitable; he explicitly disclaims proof that AI caused the growth. As small-team business examples, he reports that Emergent reached nine figures of revenue within eight months of public launch and had 15 people at $15 million annualized revenue; the auto-captioned transcript names another company as 'Retail', which he says reached $60 million annualized with about 40 people. These are reported business examples, not a comparative analysis establishing AI's contribution. Operational evidence includes his approximately 220,000-page personal wiki; overnight inbox processing, meeting preparation and research; a finance colleague turning about 100 Excel workbooks into an app; conference scheduling for 6,000 people; and an overnight synthesis of about 1,500 pages of Spinoza biographies that informed the keynote. He cites G stack's reported 123,000 GitHub stars as adoption evidence, not as a performance test. The fictional support engineer Maya illustrates alternative ownership outcomes and is not an observed displacement case. The epilepsy example is an anecdote about an 80,000-file information library, with no clinical outcome reported. The broader claims about universal knowledge-work multipliers, unprecedented revenue per person, widening competitive gaps and predictable adoption trajectories are extrapolations from these examples.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Tan presents the capability shift as already occurring in 2026, predicts practical adoption within days and compounding gains within 12 weeks, and conditions success on context quality, reusable procedures, maintenance and ownership.
pts.d: In the keynote dated 6 August 2026, Tan says almost nobody yet has the personal system he describes but that attendees could have one 'by Monday', with initial setup potentially requiring 24 hours. His proposed sequence is to run an agent tonight, begin a library over the weekend, write a skill, schedule recurring work and convert completed tasks into reusable skills. His 90-day forecast starts with clumsy, potentially time-consuming work in week one, useful contextual answers and recurring outputs by week four, and about a dozen skills plus potentially shareable tools by week 12. He predicts many will quit in week two. These are prospective adoption claims rather than reported longitudinal findings. Longer-term, he frames rented models plus owned context and an agent harness as the equation for the next decade, and predicts model improvements will increase rather than eliminate the value of context. Success requires relevant information at the right step, clear instructions and continued correction. He distinguishes model-based judgment from deterministic computation, saying databases and scripts are necessary for arithmetic and complex scheduling. He explicitly warns that uncurated memory surfaces stale facts confidently and bad skills perpetuate bad processes; provenance, contradiction checks and pruning are conditions for reliable compounding. His ownership outcome depends on who controls the repository and whether expertise can travel with the worker. In response to leakage concerns, he advocates infrastructure, repositories and keys under personal control; this is his security argument, not evidence of measured protection against leaks.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are founders and small teams, technical and nontechnical knowledge workers, employers, AI-platform users, and individuals managing complex personal information.
pts.d: For founders and startups, Tan predicts fewer staffing, funding and credential barriers, more work per person, faster experimentation and competitive pressure from agent-native rivals. He presents agents partly as augmentation of the founder's judgment and partly as a substitute workforce performing scheduled tasks with limited supervision. For developers and other knowledge workers, he predicts large output gains and a shift toward specifying, correcting and managing agent procedures. His examples explicitly include design, product management, growth, media, events and finance, extending participation to people who do not use terminals. For employees, portable skill files could accumulate career capital and support new ventures; employer-controlled files could instead let organizations retain executable expertise without retaining its originator. For users of AI platforms, he contrasts dependency on provider updates and policies with custody of personal context and procedures, while acknowledging that frontier models remain rented. For the wider public, he argues that open-source infrastructure can spread capabilities otherwise concentrated among powerful actors; the epilepsy example concerns information preparation for specialist care, not replacement of doctors or demonstrated improvement in treatment. No effect on lawyers, law firms, legal clients or access to justice is specifically asserted.
